claims.text: The target material is near-equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
The specimens are bulk polycrystalline HfNbTaTiZr ingots containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The specimens are arc-melted and homogenized.
Oxygen is incorporated interstitially in the HfNbTaTiZr alloy.
Thermal-conductivity measurements are available for oxygen-bearing HfNbTaTiZr in both the near-0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
The proposed machine-learning model will be trained using thermal-conductivity and microstructural measurements from the oxygen-containing alloy.
Interstitial oxygen produces point-defect scattering in HfNbTaTiZr.
Grain boundaries and phase distributions are relevant microstructural features for predicting the alloy's thermal conductivity.
The model explicitly represents oxygen-driven phonon scattering.
Standard analytical thermal-conductivity models for this alloy are based on ideal, defect-free crystals.
Standard analytical models neglect oxygen-related scattering and heterogeneous microstructural features.
The machine-learning model will predict thermal conductivity with errors below ±10% for 1 wt.% oxygen-bearing HfNbTaTiZr in both specified temperature regimes.
The machine-learning model will outperform traditional perfect-crystal analytical approaches.
Perfect-crystal analytical predictions commonly deviate by 20–30% or more for real HfNbTaTiZr microstructures and impurity concentrations.
The model is applicable to approximately 0–2 wt.% oxygen in near-equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
The model is valid over the continuous 0–1200 K range when the sample microstructure resembles the training data.
Predictive accuracy may degrade when oxygen content or thermal history differs significantly from the training distribution.
An independently fabricated 1 wt.% oxygen sample measured at multiple points from 550–650 K will serve as a held-out benchmark.
A prediction error greater than ±15% on the held-out 550–650 K benchmark will refute the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The central prediction requires error below ±10%, but the experiment only falsifies the hypothesis above ±15%. Errors between 10% and 15% violate the stated prediction without triggering falsification.
Training and evaluation are specified for 0–200 K and 300–1200 K, whereas the boundary claims validity over the continuous 0–1200 K range, including the unaddressed 200–300 K interval.
